rv.q: There’s not much sunshine on Leith here. Welsh, who improbably admits in the programme to being a Lionel Bart fan, has taken the best elements of the original, added some of the prequel, Skagboys, then worked with Stephen McGuinness to create new songs that energetically drive the story on, with superb choreography and a fine young cast.
Still, there is unabashed energy to the performance and the new songs, co-written by Welsh and the dance music producer Stephen McGuinness, that just about keeps the evening aloft.
But when it takes itself seriously, it's one hell of a bad trip.
Instead, it feels like a pale imitation of better iterations.

Instead, it’s ploddingly literal, often lapsing into mawkishness and soapy tedium – repeatedly ramming its social conscience down our throats, theatrically it’s almost in Blood Brothers territory, although it’s significantly less emotionally effective.
In the end, though, with the same desperation as Trainspotting’s darkest characters, you wonder what the point of it all is.
The attempt fails dismally, despite the admirable efforts of the leading man Lewis Kidd.
Sadly, the drug-addled escapades and illegal highs here look about as dangerous as a double-dose of Gaviscon.
I can’t tell you what this show wants to be but it definitely doesn’t want to be a musical.
This misfiring adaptation is the perfect case in point that not every story should be turned into a musical.
The newly-written songs are no match for New Order, Primal Scream, Pulp or Blur, though the cast do Tears for Fears’ “Mad World” and The Verve’s “Bitter Sweet Symphony” for good measure.

So what results is a kind of hybrid jukebox show, one that at points almost feels like a 90s nostalgia fest, but makes an awkward vehicle for a bleak story of broken characters seeking highs against a backdrop of urban decline.
While it has some redeeming features, Trainspotting The Musical sadly has more lows than highs.
Go if you must, but don't say you weren't warned.
What they will find instead is a dramatically muddled retelling that strips away everything which made the original so vital.
Ultimately it’s the ineptitude rather than the tricky subject matter that sinks Trainspotting The Musical.
Overall, Trainspotting the Musical should not be missed by any fans of the book or film, or anyone who wants to see a show which balances between tragedy, comedy, political inspection and art forms.
Trainspotting The Musical achieves that elusive high of transforming abject human misery into an evening of sharply crafted entertainment.
Trainspotting the Musical is one long example of gluttony, a show that dines out on its own greatness and ends up eating itself on the process.
Like that final act of theft, Trainspotting feels like an unsatisfying cash grab that leaves everyone feeling robbed.
As it stands, the show never quite decides whether it wants to interrogate addiction and deprivation or simply borrow their imagery for texture and that indecision is fatal.
There's no such vision here, no real aspiration beyond filling up a bingo card of scenes that made us smile back in 1996.
Choose the genius immersive play that blows away this self-serving spin-off that any self-respecting Scot would likely label 'pure shite'.
I’ll be blunt when I say this is without a doubt the worst show in the West End this year, and a contender for the biggest train wreck ever seen on a West End stage.
This musical adaptation feels authentic to the original while also fleshing out Renton’s backstory.

cn.t: Critics savage this ill-conceived adaptation, calling it leaden and misconceived where Welsh's novel was edgy and vital. The musical strips away the source material's jagged wit and dangerous energy, leaving mawkish tedium in its place.
